title: Claymation FPS with Gemini Neon!
author: AntiqueFeedback7447
selftext:
Built a claymation style FPS with Gemini Neon, medium effort agents! Its honestly a good model to work with!

You can try to beat it at [https://claycalypse.vercel.app/](https://claycalypse.vercel.app/) 

\- Procedural claymation SDF bodies that allow for chunking and shooting off clay mass, including limbs, face etc.  
\- Stepped claymation animation for the enemies to get a bit more of a "stop motion" feel  
\- Partly destructible environment and props  
\- Multiple enemy types with procedural IK movement, including a final boss in "Hell Mode" :D   
\- Claymation weapon and hand + rig and animations for punch, shoot and reload. 

Took about one foundation and 7 polishing sessions on the first day. Followed up with a few more gameplay polishes on the second day. The model does need its fair share of guidance, but if prompted well it implements fairly quickly and with good output quality! 3D capabilities are also great!  
  
Issue experienced with Neon that were a bit annoying:

* Gets stuck often in thinking/editing loops? Evaluating its own performance metrics?
* Ignores answering questions/input while working sometimes
* Random “abort” errors
* Context window seems to fill up quite quickly (tested mostly with the 300K window)
* Seems to randomly slow down, waiting ages for small edits

Other than that, it picks up design and gameplay concepts quickly once established and follows them well!

replies.author: AntiqueFeedback7447
replies.body:
Hey! I promise you it was "just" me prompting Neon in Cursor :D At this point of AI progress, it all comes down to knowing what to prompt for, how to breakdown "game feel". 

In terms of animations, what you see is a few separate models:  
\- For left arm, its left hand + wrist and separately the coat.   
\- For the right its the weapon + mirrored hand.

Neon did a pretty good job at modelling and rigging a claymation hand. Good thing about the claymation style i went for, it can look a bit ugly :D With neon I then just spun-up a small custom editor, where I could adjust finger positions and adjust keyframe positions for the reload animation. 

Same for the shotgun, its few separate pieces, so it can be bent and reloaded.

For the first person movement feel + shoot feel its the classics:  
\- subtle bob  
\- fov + camera punch shake   
\- lean in dash direction  
\- vignette effects when taking damage  
\- nuzzle + smoke vfx at shotgun barrel end  
  
From there you can then go and refine :) There's lots of info on the web around how to make "shooting a gun" or "running in an FPS view" feel better. Always do some research, either by yourself or even just by prompting your model to do the research first before implementation, helps a ton!

replies.author: w1zinvestmentss
replies.body: Good for you. Sounds like you did quite a bit of work and research. And it wasn't just one shoted. Is this possible by prompting? Or you need to use agents working to together. My apologies, I use antigravity not cursor. Like to know what is possible.

replies.author: AntiqueFeedback7447
replies.body:
Yes definitely achievable with prompting! But I did break it down in multiple separate dedicated sessions. And within one session, there were definitely more than one iteration included. Not sure how Antigravity works, but within a session in Cursor, your main agent you are talking to is capable of using sub-agents. So usually i instruct to make use of a small dedicated game dev team of subagents, to cover the session topic in-depth, one agent covering a specific discipline of the sessions design goal. For example I ran one session on polishing the gameplay feel of the clay bodies. one agent was refining/tweaking the procedural limb movement, while the other looked into clay material variations and the other refined the procedural SDF body approach to achieve one seamless and chunkable "clay body".

So I can highly recommend you to split up your work across multiple sessions, and even across multiple agents within one session if that session has a larger deliverable.

What I always do though at the start of every project is a "planning" session. Plan out your idea first, into multiple work packages. Then you can implement your prototype one work package at a time, or even parallelise them if you feel comfortable with it.

replies.author: AntiqueFeedback7447
replies.body:
Not sure how much the 20$ plan can sustain, but I’d encourage you to try its limitations 😁 Usually you will probably have limits within one day and within a whole week. 

The one thing you need to be mindful of is the thinking level that is set for your model. I highly recommend starting and using Neon on medium effort, or even low for small tasks. Especially if you have things planned out in advance and the deliverables are clear, low and medium effort work perfectly, saves you tokens and time. Very very rarely I make use of High effort nowadays. Both Opus and Neon are amazing at medium effort. Carbon and Fable are too token hungry, take longer, and I didnt see that crazy of an uplift in output.

replies.author: AntiqueFeedback7447
replies.body: Totally! It did take me some iterations and around 3 dedicated sessions to get to the final look. Had to also look at some references to understand how to get a better "rough shaped" clay look. Initially the clay material was too smooth, glossy, and creatures were not built out of one mold only, but had separate limbs stuck together, visibly leaving seams and not actually looking or behaving fully procedural. In the end we found a way to build everything out of "one mold" using SDF and then applying the custom material to it. But most of this just by prompting with clear directions to try, doing multiple variations and tests and then align from there :)
